title: US-backed vaccine trial on babies canceled after international outcry
gist: On October 16, Guinea-Bissau's Council of Ministers formally rejected a US CDC-funded ($1.6 million) trial by Denmark's Bandim Health Project that would have withheld the hepatitis B newborn vaccine dose from half the participants. Judicial police then searched Bandim's offices and sealed its vaccine stock. The WHO and outside experts had condemned the trial, backed by RFK Jr.'s CDC, as unethical under the Declaration of Helsinki. The researchers, who are under Danish misconduct investigation, blame the backlash on "Anglophone media" and say the trial will not be moved elsewhere.

insights.claim: Guinea-Bissau's Council of Ministers formally reaffirmed its rejection on October 16 of a US-funded clinical trial, run by Danish researchers, that was looking for alleged nonspecific harms from the newborn hepatitis B vaccine dose.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: A setback for the RFK Jr.-era HHS effort to produce evidence questioning vaccines.

themes.theme: Ethics dispute over withholding the birth dose

insights.claim: The WHO and many outside experts call the hepatitis B trial unethical because it would withhold the newborn dose from half the participants. Given Guinea-Bissau's high rates of chronic hepatitis B, that would put thousands of babies at risk of lifelong infection leading to cirrhosis, liver cancer and premature death.

insights.so_what: Global health bodies are resisting US-backed vaccine skepticism.

insights.claim: Bandim's researchers argue the hepatitis B trial was ethical because Guinea-Bissau does not currently give routine birth doses, so control infants would not have been vaccinated anyway. The country, which had a coup in November 2025, plans to introduce a birth dose in 2028 but lacks the resources now.

insights.claim: The WHO cites the Declaration of Helsinki, which requires that trial participants receive the best proven intervention regardless of the local standard. For hepatitis B, that is the newborn dose given within 24 hours of birth. The WHO says resource constraints cannot justify withholding proven care in research.
insights.speaker: World Health Organization
insights.so_what: The ethics standard that blocks this kind of trial design; useful context for future disputes over trials funded by the Kennedy-era HHS.

themes.theme: US CDC funding under RFK Jr.

insights.claim: In December the US CDC awarded an unsolicited $1.6 million grant to Bandim Health, which is run by Christine Stabell Benn and her husband Peter Aaby, for the hepatitis B trial. After Guinea-Bissau reportedly halted the trial in January, the CDC under Robert F. Kennedy Jr. reportedly set aside another $1.6 million to push ahead.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Shows HHS directing grants toward vaccine-skeptic research, a policy-risk signal for vaccine makers.

insights.claim: Bandim researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn study nonspecific harms from vaccines and have been praised by anti-vaccine advocates including RFK Jr. Their scientific peers criticize the quality of their work, and Danish authorities are investigating them for alleged scientific misconduct.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: The research behind HHS-backed vaccine skepticism has questionable credibility.

insights.claim: Bandim researcher Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer blames the backlash on "Anglophone media." He says the coverage fueled rumors in Guinea-Bissau that the Americans were testing a novel, dangerous vaccine and that Bissau-Guinean newborns were treated as disposable, which damaged trust in the hepatitis B vaccine.

insights.so_what: Controversial trials can damage vaccine confidence in host countries, a risk for global immunization programs.
